summary: Clarifies the concept of intent in networking and gives an overview of the functionality associated with it. The terms are often used loosely or confused with ideas such as policy, and the document aims to build a common understanding. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Intent is the difference between saying what you want the network to achieve and saying how to achieve it. This RFC pins the word down, explains how it differs from a rule and from a service description, and describes the two halves of a system that works this way: the part that carries out the intent, and the part that keeps checking that the network still does what was asked.

questions: how is intent different from policy
what does an intent-based system do
how is intent different from a policy rule
what are intent fulfillment and intent assurance
subtitle: What intent means in network management, and how it differs from policy and from a service model.

tldr.problem: The word intent is used loosely in networking and is often confused with policy, with service models, or with a high-level API, so people who use it mean different things.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9315 defines intent as operational goals and outcomes expressed declaratively, without saying how to achieve them, and sets out the functionality an intent-based system needs: fulfillment, which makes it happen, and assurance, which keeps it true.
tldr.outcome: The document gives the research community a shared vocabulary for intent-based networking, separates intent from policy and service models, and lists the principles such a system should follow.

facts.value: Operational goals and outcomes, stated declaratively, without specifying how

today: RFC 9315 is an Informational document published in October 2022 by the IRTF Network Management Research Group, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a concepts and definitions document: the security and architecture detail it points to lives in later documents, and the document itself notes that more thorough security analysis is needed as the technology matures.

sections.title: Why the Word Needed Defining
sections.content:
This document is a product of the IRTF Network Management Research Group and reflects the consensus of the group. Interest in management and operations in the IETF has focused on individual network and device features, with standardization emphasis on instrumentation that a device must provide, such as SNMP-based management and the more than 200 MIBs the IETF has defined, and on YANG data models for things such as interface configuration, access control list configuration and Syslog configuration.

Managing networks by configuring myriads of individual settings on a device-by-device basis is no longer an option in modern environments. It is hard to keep device configurations consistent across a network and consistent with the services they are meant to enable, to adapt the network quickly, and to do any of that at scale. Operations also need to be streamlined and automated wherever possible, to lower cost, to allow rapid reconfiguration at sub-second time scales, and to ensure that networks are delivering their functionality as expected. That requires the ability to consume operational data, perform analytics and take context-aware actions at near real-time speeds.

The IETF has therefore begun to address end-to-end management that goes beyond individual devices in isolation, with examples such as YANG models for network topology and the service models used by service orchestration systems and controllers. Much of the interest comes from work on autonomic networks, which aim to lower operational expenses and make management of the network as a whole more straightforward. Autonomic networks are still intended to exhibit self-management properties, yet they require input from an operator or outside system to provide operational guidance about the goals, purposes and service instances the network is to serve. That input is what is commonly called intent. A network that accepts such input is an Intent-Based Network (IBN), and a system that helps implement intent is an Intent-Based System (IBS). Such systems can take many forms: a controller or management system running as an application on a server, or a set of functions distributed across the network that collectively perform the intent-based functionality.

Intent is about more than a nicer form of operator interaction with higher-level abstractions. It is about letting operators focus on the outcomes they want and leaving the detail of how those outcomes are achieved to the IBN or IBS. Working at the level of outcomes gives greater efficiency and flexibility at greater scale, in shorter time scales, and with less dependence on human activity, and therefore fewer opportunities for mistakes. It also makes intent-based networking a natural candidate for artificial intelligence techniques that could bring the next level of network automation.

The idea is not entirely new. The ITU-T Telecommunications Management Network model introduced management layers for network element, network, service and business management, with high-level objectives propagating top down; the abstraction hierarchy there was crucial for decomposing management complexity. Policy-Based Network Management has long made the case for specifying high-level management policies that policy systems then render into low-level configuration and control logic. What has been missing is putting these concepts into a current context. This document clarifies the concepts behind intent, differentiates intent from related concepts, and provides an overview of first-order principles and associated functionality, with the goal of contributing to a common and shared understanding.
sections.plainLanguage: Configuring every device by hand does not scale, and the IETF has been adding models for whole networks rather than single boxes. The idea of intent is the next step up: an operator says what should be true of the network, and the system works out the steps. The word was being used loosely, so this RFC fixes its meaning and separates it from the neighbouring ideas.

sections.title: What Intent Is
sections.content:
Intent is defined as a set of operational goals, that is what a network is supposed to meet, and outcomes, that is what a network is supposed to deliver, defined in a declarative manner without specifying how to achieve or implement them. The term was first introduced for autonomic networks, where it means an abstract, high-level policy used to operate the network, a specific type of policy that a user provides to guide a network that would otherwise run without human intervention. To avoid using intent as a synonym for policy, the document introduces a clear distinction.

Intent is purely declarative: it says what to accomplish, not how. Two abstractions follow. It provides data abstraction, so users need not be concerned with low-level device configuration. And it provides functional abstraction from particular management and control logic, so users need not be concerned even with how to achieve a given intent; the desired outcome is specified and the IBS works out a course of action, using an algorithm or a set of rules derived from the intent.

The document gives examples of intent, expressed in natural language for clarity: steer traffic originating from endpoints in one geography away from a second geography unless the destination lies there; avoid routing traffic from a given set of endpoints through a particular vendor's equipment even at the expense of reduced service levels; maximize network utilization even if it means trading off service levels such as latency and loss, unless service levels have deteriorated 20% or more from their historical mean; ensure VPN services have path protection at all times for all paths; generate in situ OAM data and network telemetry for later offline analysis whenever significant fluctuations in latency across a path are observed; route traffic in a Space Information Network in a way that minimizes dependency on stratospheric balloons unless the intended destination is an aircraft; and, for a smart city service, ensure traffic signal control traffic uses dedicated and redundant slices that avoid fate sharing.

By contrast, these would not be intent: configuring a given interface with an IP address, which is device configuration; a rule that emits an alert when interface utilization exceeds a threshold, which can help automation but is a simple rule; configuring a VPN with a tunnel from A to B over path P, which is a service configuration; and denying traffic to prefix P1 unless it is traffic from prefix P2, which is an access policy or firewall rule.

Ideally the network itself would render intent, translating it into device-specific rules and courses of action, and would disseminate it across all devices, which can then decide whether they need to act on it. That decentralization will not be practical in all cases: users may require a single conceptual point of interaction with the network, which acts as the operational front end and manages other systems to realize the intent; most devices remain intent-agnostic and focused on forwarding; many devices are constrained in processing resources; and realizing some kinds of intent benefits from global knowledge of the network that individual devices cannot maintain. Certain functionality therefore has to be provided by specialized functions, which may still be distributed even when conceptually centralized. A network that can be managed this way is an IBN: it recognizes and ingests intent, configures and adapts itself accordingly, and reaches the intended outcome without the user specifying the technical steps. An IBS is a system that lets users manage a network using intent, serving as their point of interaction and implementing the functionality needed.

The document also warns against intent-washing, the temptation to broaden the term and paint other concepts in a new light by renaming them, such as calling the northbound interface of an SDN controller an intent interface. It distinguishes four subcategories. Operational intent defines the operational goals of an operator, and corresponds to the intent of this document. Rule intent is a synonym for policy rules about what to do when certain events occur. Service intent is a synonym for a customer service model. Flow intent is a synonym for a service level objective for a given flow.
sections.plainLanguage: Intent states the destination, not the route. "Keep this service within its latency target" is intent. "Set this interface's address" and "alert me when this link is 80% busy" are not, because they are instructions rather than outcomes. The document also warns against renaming ordinary interfaces as intent.

sections.title: Intent, Policy and Service Models
sections.content:
Service models. A service model represents a service provided by a network to a user, describing a service and its parameters in a portable and implementation-agnostic way. Two subcategories are distinguished: a Customer Service Model describes an instance of a service as provided to a customer, possibly associated with a service order, and a Service Delivery Model describes how a service is instantiated over existing networking infrastructure. Examples of a service are a Layer 3 VPN, a network slice or residential Internet access. Service models represent service instances as entities in their own right, with their own parameters, actions and life cycles, typically bound to end users who might be billed for the service.

Instantiating a service involves several aspects: a user or northbound system defines or requests the service; resources such as IP addresses, AS numbers, VLAN or VxLAN pools, interfaces, bandwidth or memory are allocated; the mapping of services onto those resources is defined, often with several possible mappings whose selection depends on context; bindings between upper- and lower-level objects are maintained; and the operational state of the service is validated and assured. Realizing service models involves a system such as a controller that provides provisioning logic, breaking down high-level service abstractions into device abstractions, allocating resources and orchestrating provisioning steps. Orchestration is generally conducted with a push model: the controller initiates the operations, pushes configurations down and validates that the new state was accepted and is in sync with the desired state. Updating, modifying and decommissioning services have to be supported too, and the device remains agnostic to the service and to the fact that its configuration is part of one. Unlike intent, service models do not allow a desired outcome to be defined that an IBS would maintain automatically; managing them requires sophisticated algorithms and control logic from providers or system integrators.

Policy and Policy-Based Network Management. Policy-Based Network Management separates the rules that govern the behaviour of a system from the functionality of the system, promising lower maintenance costs and better flexibility and runtime adaptability. A policy is a set of rules governing the choices in behaviour of a system, and a rule typically consists of an event whose occurrence triggers it, a set of conditions that must be true before the actions fire, and the actions to carry out. Policy-based management is an imperative paradigm: policies specify precisely what needs to be done, when, and in which circumstance, which makes management a set of simple control loops. Policies usually involve abstraction to cope with heterogeneous devices: rather than device-specific events, conditions and actions, the policy is defined over a canonical model, and a policy agent on a controller or device renders it into a device-specific representation. That decoupling of definition from instantiation and enforcement lets the same policy be applied across many devices, and lets operators think above device specifics. PBNM is typically push-based, with a manager or controller deploying policies and monitoring them, though other architectures exist, including a pull component where a Policy Decision Point, which may live outside the managed device and have global visibility, decides what action to take when a device cannot reach a conclusion itself; the device then acts as a Policy Enforcement Point.

Like intent, policies provide a higher layer of abstraction, but the rules and courses of action still have to be articulated by users. Because the intent is unknown to the policy system, conflict resolution within or between policies requires interaction with a user or logic outside PBNM. In that sense policy is a lower level of abstraction than intent, and it is conceivable for an IBS to generate policies that a PBNM system then deploys.

The document summarises the differences. A service model is a data model describing service instances provided to customers, with dependencies on lower-level device and network models; instantiating it requires orchestration by a system, and the orchestration logic is not part of the model. Policy is a set of rules, typically modelled around events, conditions and actions, expressing simple control loops that devices can render without outside intervention; it lets users define what to do under what circumstances but not the desired outcome. Intent is a high-level declarative goal operating at the level of the network and the services it provides rather than individual devices, used to define outcomes and operational goals without saying how they should be achieved and without enumerating events, conditions and actions; the algorithm or rules to apply can be derived by the IBS, and in the autonomic case intent is ideally rendered by the network itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Three words travel together and are often swapped. A service model describes a service a customer buys. A policy is a rule that says what to do when something happens. Intent is the outcome the network should reach, with the how left to the system. The document draws the line by asking who supplies the missing detail: the user supplies it for policy and service models, the system works it out for intent.

sections.title: Principles of an Intent-Based System
sections.content:
The document lists six main operating principles that characterise the intent-based, intent-driven or intent-defined nature of a system.

  1. Single Source of Truth (SSoT) and Single Version of Truth (SVoT). The SSoT is an essential component of an IBS. The set of validated intent expressions is the system's single source of truth. Together with records of operational states it allows the intended and actual states to be compared and the drift between them determined, and that drift is the basis for corrective actions. If the IBS can predict states it can anticipate diverging trends and act to minimise their impact. SSoT also gives traceability, so it can be checked whether the original intent and business goals were met, and the effect of changes to intent parameters can be evaluated. The Single Version of Truth derives from the SSoT and supports operations such as querying, polling or filtering measured and correlated information to create views for users. In other contexts SSoT is also referred to as the invariance of the intent.
  2. One touch but not one shot. In an ideal IBS the user expresses intent in one form or another and the system takes over all subsequent operations. A zero-touch approach could be imagined where the IBS recognises intentions in any form of data, but that should not distract from the fact that reaching a well-formed and valid intent expression is not a one-shot process. The interface between user and IBS can be interactive and iterative: intent expressions may initially contain implicit parts and imprecise or unknown parameters and constraints, and the role of the IBS is to parse, understand and refine them until they are well formed and can be used for fulfillment and assurance. Refinement can involve the user validating the proposed refinement and being asked for clarifications where parameters cannot be deduced, and the IBS also has to moderate between conflicting intent, helping users choose between alternatives with different ramifications.
  3. Autonomy and supervision. The dual principle allows a system with the autonomy to conduct its tasks without user intervention, taking its own decisions within its areas of concern on how to meet user expectations for performance and quality, while providing the proper level of supervision to satisfy user requirements for reporting and escalation.
  4. Learning. An IBS is a learning system. Where the user of an event-condition-action policy defines the expected behaviour beforehand, in an IBS the user only declares what the system is supposed to achieve. This transfers reasoning from the human to the system, and implies capabilities for learning, reasoning and knowledge representation and management. Learning can apply to optimisation of the intent rendering or of the refinement process, and since an IBS is continuously evolving, the conditions for continuous learning are created. Planning can also be leveraged to anticipate future system state and elaborate plans that accommodate changes in intent or network conditions while preserving stability and efficiency.
  5. Capability exposure. Expressive network capabilities, requirements and constraints are needed so that intent can be composed and decomposed and user expectations mapped onto system capabilities.
  6. Abstract and outcome-driven. Users need not be concerned with how intent is achieved and can think in terms of outcomes and higher-level concepts independent of vendor-specific renderings.

The document adds further considerations. Intent targets are not individual devices but typically aggregations, such as groups of devices with a common role, or abstractions such as service types, service instances or topologies. There is abstraction and inherent virtualization, being agnostic to implementation details. Human-tailored network interaction means the IBN should speak the user's language rather than requiring the user to speak the device's. Explainability is an important function, together with detection and resolution of conflicting intent and reconciliation of what the user wants against what the network can actually do. And there must be inherent support, verification and assurance of trust.
sections.plainLanguage: Six principles describe what makes a system intent-based. It keeps one validated copy of the intent and compares reality against it. It asks the user for what it needs once, then works on its own. It stays out of the operator's way but still reports. It learns how to satisfy the intent better over time. It knows what the network can actually do. And it stays in outcome terms rather than device terms.

sections.title: Fulfillment, Assurance and the Life Cycle
sections.content:
The functionality of intent-based networking divides into two categories. Intent fulfillment provides the functions and interfaces that let users communicate intent to the network and that take the actions needed to ensure the intent is achieved. It includes algorithms that determine proper courses of action and functions that learn to optimize outcomes over time, the orchestration of coordinated configuration operations across the network, and the rendering of higher-level abstractions into lower-level parameters and control knobs. Intent assurance provides the functions and interfaces that let users validate and monitor that the network is indeed adhering to and complying with intent. This is needed to assess the effectiveness of the fulfillment actions, providing feedback that allows those functions to be trained or tuned over time, and it is needed to address intent drift, where a system originally meets the intent but over time its behaviour changes until it no longer does, or does so less effectively.

Fulfillment has three sets of functions. Intent ingestion and interaction with users covers obtaining intent through interaction with users, recognising intent from that interaction, and letting users refine and articulate it so that it becomes actionable. These functions go beyond a non-intent-based API, though such APIs may still be needed for interactions with other machines. Many cases involve intuitive workflows that guide users through ingestion and make sure all inputs needed for intent modelling and translation have been gathered, and they may support unconventional human-machine interaction in which a dialog provides clarifications, explains ramifications and trade-offs, and facilitates refinements. The goal is for IBSs to be easy and natural to use, without a steep learning curve that forces the user to learn the language of the system.

Intent translation turns user intent into courses of action and requests against the network that are meaningful to configuration and provisioning systems. These functions sit at the core of an IBS, bridging the gap between user interaction and the management side that orchestrates provisioning across the network. Beyond breaking a higher abstraction down into policies and device configuration, translation can be complemented by functions and algorithms that optimise and that learn and improve over time, so that the best outcomes are reached where several ways of achieving them are conceivable. Satisfying an intent may involve computing paths and other parameters to be configured across the network, and the heuristics and algorithms for doing so may evolve as network conditions change. Intent orchestration then deals with the actual configuration and provisioning steps that have to be orchestrated across the network, as determined by translation.

Assurance has four sets of functions. Monitoring observes the network and its exhibited behaviour: watching for events and performance outliers, measuring service levels being delivered, and generating and collecting telemetry. Monitoring is the basis for the next set. Intent compliance assessment compares the monitored behaviour with the intended behaviour held in the SSoT, continuously assessing and validating whether the observations show compliance, including assessing the effectiveness of fulfillment actions by verifying that they had the desired effect and how large that effect was, and analysing and aggregating raw observation data. The results can feed back into the learning functions that optimise outcomes. Compliance assessment also looks for intent drift over time, which can be caused by control plane or lower-level management operations that inadvertently change behaviour in conflict with earlier intent, and needs to detect when drift occurs or is about to occur and assess its severity. Intent compliance actions trigger corrective action when drift occurs or behaviour is inconsistent with the intent, resolving the drift and bringing the network back into compliance, or, where necessary, triggering reporting that alerts operators and gives them the information and tools to react, for example by helping them articulate modifications to the original intent to moderate between conflicting concerns. Abstraction, aggregation and reporting report the outcome back to the user in ways that relate to their intent, which means analysing, aggregating and abstracting the observations so that lower-level concepts such as detailed performance statistics and low-level settings are uplifted to concepts the user can relate to and act on, with compliance status reported and adequately summarised and visualised.

Intent also has a life cycle: it comes into being, may change over time, and may at some point be retracted. The document's diagram divides the functions into two horizontal planes, fulfillment and assurance, and three vertical spaces. The User Space holds the functions that let users articulate intent and let the IBS recognise it, and that report the status of the network relative to the intent. The Translation, or Intent-Based System Space bridges users and the network operations infrastructure: translating intent into a course of action, planning and optimising those courses of action in light of feedback, analysing and aggregating observations to validate compliance and take corrective action, and abstracting observations so they relate to the intent as users expressed it. The Network Operations Space holds the orchestration, configuration, monitoring and measurement functions that effectuate the rendered intent and observe its effects.

Two cycles emerge. The inner intent control loop between the IBS and the network operations space is completely autonomic, with no human in the loop: it is closed-loop automation that validates intent against observations, feeds them into the planning of the rendering so that the configuration can be adjusted, and counteracts intent drift. It also allows the effectiveness of actions to be assessed so that the rendering of intent can be learned and improved. The outer loop extends to the user space, where the user takes action and adjusts their intent based on observations and feedback from the IBS.
sections.plainLanguage: The work splits in two. Fulfillment takes the intent and acts on it: work out a plan, translate it into device settings, push the settings out. Assurance watches the result, compares it with the intent, and either corrects the difference or tells the operator about it. Between them they form a loop that runs without the operator, with a second, slower loop that lets the operator change the intent itself.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because this document describes concepts and definitions, its security considerations stay high level, in the form of principles, guidelines and requirements; the detailed analysis belongs in the documents that specify the architecture and functionality.

Security in intent-based networking applies to different facets: securing the IBS itself, mitigating the effects of erroneous, harmful or compromised intent statements, and expressing security policies or security-related parameters with intent statements.

Securing the IBS aims at making it operationally secure through security mechanisms and best practices, which may consist of intent verification and validation, allowing operations on intent only by authenticated and authorised users, and protection against or detection of tampered statements of intent. It may also include multiple levels of intent, where intent related to securing the network occurs at a deeper level that overrides other levels if necessary and cannot be modified through regular operations but only through specifically secured ones. Explanation components that describe the security ramifications and trade-offs should also be considered.

Mitigating the effects of erroneous or compromised statements aims at making the IBS operationally safe through checkpoint and safeguard mechanisms and operating principles: the ability to detect unintended, detrimental or abnormal behaviour automatically; the ability to roll back or fall back to a previous safe state automatically and gracefully; the ability to prevent or contain error amplification, which comes from combining a higher degree of automation with the intrinsic higher degree of freedom, ambiguity and implicit information conveyed by intent statements; and dynamic levels of supervision and reporting so the user has the right information at the right time with the right context. Erroneous or harmful intent statements may inadvertently propagate and compromise security, and compromised statements, for example forged by an inside attacker, may sabotage or harm network resources and make them vulnerable to further, larger attacks, for instance by defeating certain security mechanisms.

Expressing security policies or security-related parameters through the intent formalism covers data governance, levels of confidentiality in data exchange, levels of availability of system resources and of protection in forwarding paths and isolation in processing functions, levels of encryption, and authorised entities for given operations.

The document ends with a balanced note. Deploying intent-based networking in operational environments will create new security concerns, which have to be anticipated at design and specification time. It may also be an enabler for better security: security and privacy rules could be expressed in a more human-friendly and generic way, be less technology specific and less complex, and lead to fewer low-level configuration mistakes, and the detection of threats or attacks could become simpler and more comprehensive thanks to conflict detection at a higher level or coarser granularity. More thorough security analyses should be conducted as the understanding of the technology matures.
sections.plainLanguage: An intent that is wrong, or that an attacker has rewritten, is dangerous precisely because the system acts on it without checking with a person. So the document asks for validation of intent before it is acted on, a way back to a known good state, and protection against one bad statement damaging the whole network.

viz.caption: THE SIX OPERATING PRINCIPLES OF AN INTENT-BASED SYSTEM

items.title: Single Source of Truth
items.text: The validated intent expressions are kept in one place, so the intended state and the actual state can be compared and the drift acted on.

items.title: One touch, not one shot
items.text: The user expresses intent once; refining it into a valid form is an iterative dialogue, not a single submission.

items.title: Autonomy and supervision
items.text: The system acts on its own within its scope, while still reporting and escalating what the user needs to know.

items.title: Learning
items.text: The system works out how to satisfy the intent, and improves that method over time as conditions change.

items.title: Capability exposure
items.text: The system knows what the network can actually do, so it can compose and decompose intent accordingly.

items.title: Abstract and outcome-driven
items.text: Users work in outcomes and in their own vocabulary, not in device settings.
